_comment: Sapient species and the polities they build. The bestiary's opposite number: anything here is a people, and the validator refuses to let a name appear in both files. Provenance works differently from the replicant tree — species and governments have no parents, so the tier letters don't transfer. What's graded instead is whether the books state a thing or leave it open: an acronym is only expanded here if a character expands it on the page.

entries.name: Humans
entries.note: The species the Bobs used to be, and the one they keep having to negotiate with. By book 4 humanity is spread across enough systems that its politics are interstellar rather than national, and the Bobs' relationship to it has drifted from 'us' to something more like a founding generation nobody asked for.

entries.name: Deltans
entries.note: Pre-industrial hunter-gatherers, and the reason the Prime Directive argument runs through the whole series. Bob found them losing a war of attrition to the gorilloids, decided that watching was also a choice, and started handing over better spears. They call him Bawbe. Their word for a family group is hexghi — roughly 'families of our fire' — which is worth knowing because it looks like a species name and isn't.

entries.name: Quinlans
entries.note: The otter-shaped inhabitants of the Heaven's River megastructure, and the most-mentioned people in the books. The Bobs called them Snarks first — Garfield's joke, since they already had Boojums — and Bob insisted the name was provisional until they learned what the Quinlans call themselves. They did. That is the whole ethic of the series in one exchange.

entries.name: Pav
entries.note: Found industrialising hard — Victorian-equivalent, and pumping smoke into their own atmosphere at a rate that made their survival an open question. Jacques named them by elimination: Deltans was taken, Pavonians sounded terrible, so Pav for now. It stuck. They later declined to join the UFS, which the Bobs had gone to the trouble of naming non-human-centrically on the assumption that they would.

entries.name: the Others
entries.note:
Strip-miners of whole systems, and the only species in the books the Bobs fought a war against rather than argued about. Their method was to arrive, consume everything usable including the inhabitants, and move on — which is what turns the Bobs from explorers into a defence force. The name is a placeholder that stopped being one.

Bill puts a composite scan image of one in front of the moot in Bk2 ch57, and it is the most detailed physical description of any species in the books. About four feet, never standing straight, shading from an oily green-violet sheen through grey to black. He tells the room to start from a gorilla's posture — not quite on four limbs, not quite upright — with front limbs like meaty wings ending in thick suckered digits for gripping prey rather than handling tools, and a back end he compares to a sea lion's with a tail added to a split one. The front opens in a vertical slash into a maw that grinds and strips rather than chews, with dexterous feeding fingers folding out of it. The head carries the senses and a ring of small eyes around its dome for vision in every direction, while what appears to be the brain sits high on the trunk instead. The scans also showed them packed at the density of a crowded room throughout the living space, which is what settles the hive reading.

entries.name: FAITH
entries.cite: Bk1 ch4 · Bob, July 15, 2133; Bk2 · List of Terms
entries.note: The theocracy that owned Bob's frozen head, and the state whose information policy denied him his own family records — under FAITH, nothing is public by default. No character ever unpacks the acronym, and this register recorded that gap for as long as it was true. The List of Terms at the back of book 2 expands it, which is Taylor rather than a character but is still printed in the novel. Recorded now with that distinction rather than the gap.

entries.name: USE
entries.note: One of the powers of Bob's second lifetime, and expanded on the page by Dr. Landers. Bob's opinion was that the name was grandiose given how little of Eurasia it covered; Landers pointed out that the old USA hadn't covered all of America either.

entries.name: Brazilian Empire
entries.note: A rival power of the same era, and one of the states whose competing colony ships turned the launch window into a shooting match. Sparsely mentioned but consequential: the war it takes part in is what leaves Earth uninhabitable.

entries.name: VEHEMENT
entries.expansion: Voluntary Extinction of Human Existence Means Earth's Natural Transformation
entries.note: Anti-human extremists who held that humanity had had its chance and should be allowed to die out — and who were prepared to help. Colonel Butterworth supplies the expansion and immediately undercuts it: that, or something close to it, he had heard several variants and one or two obscene ones. The expansion is recorded here with that hedge intact, because the hedge is the citation.

entries.name: the Spits
entries.note: A survivor enclave on Spitsbergen, led by Gudmund Valter, and one of the groups Riker had to ration a dying planet between. Their island was likely to become uninhabitable first, which gave every conversation with them a deadline. Easy to mistake for a species from the word alone; it is a place with people on it.

entries.name: UFS
entries.note: The interstellar federation of the later books, whose name the Bobs deliberately kept free of anything human-centric so that other species could join without feeling annexed. The Pav declined anyway. Will's summary of the resulting council sessions is not printable in a family register.

entries.name: Pangean Council
entries.note: The colonial government that formally went to war with a faction of the Bobiverse. Its statement is careful to describe Starfleet as devices rather than people, and to call the name disparaging — a government drawing the personhood line exactly where it finds convenient, which is the same line the Bobs spend five books arguing about from the other side.

entries.name: the Administrator
entries.note: The governing power inside Heaven's River, enforcing a set of rules called the Limits. Quinlans discuss it the way people discuss weather that can evict them — fairness is explicitly not part of its vocabulary, and it cannot be stopped, only avoided. Whether it counts as a government, a maintenance system or a person is left open.

entries.name: Quinlan Resistance
entries.note: Quinlans organised against the Administrator and the Limits. They matter to the argument the books are making: a people the Bobs first labelled Snarks turn out to have their own politics, their own factions and their own dissidents, none of which needed outside help to exist.
